title: 5 · Classes & Objects (Deep Dive)
learn:
The story

You run a pizza shop. Every pizza has a size, toppings and a price, and every pizza can be baked and sliced. You do not invent the idea of a pizza from scratch each time. You keep one recipe card. In Java, that recipe card is a class. Each real pizza you bake from it is an object.

Class vs object, properly

A class is a blueprint: it describes the fields (data, the pizza's size) and methods (behaviour, bake()). It holds no real data itself. An object is a real instance built with new. Many objects can come from one class and each keeps its own copy of the fields. Changing one pizza's toppings never touches another pizza.

Fields

Fields are variables declared inside the class but outside any method. They are the object's memory, its state.

The constructor, the object's birth certificate

When you write new Pizza(...), Java builds the object and instantly runs its constructor. Four rules to tattoo on your brain: (1) same name as the class, (2) no return type, not even void, (3) runs automatically with new, (4) if you write none, Java secretly gives you an empty one. The moment you write any constructor yourself, the free empty one disappears. Write several constructors with different parameters and that is constructor overloading.

this: the object pointing at itself

Inside a method, this means the object currently running the code. Its main job: separating a field from a parameter with the same name. this.size = size; reads: store the parameter inside this object's field. Write size = size; and you assign the parameter to itself, the field stays at its default, and your program silently misbehaves. this(...) can also call another constructor in the same class, which saves repeating code.

Encapsulation: the vending machine

A vending machine hides its insides and gives you buttons. You cannot reach in and grab the snacks. That is encapsulation: fields are private, access happens through public getters and setters. The setter can protect the data, for example refusing a GPA of 500. This is the single most examined idea in class questions.

Memory: references, not boxes

With Student s1 = new Student(...), the variable s1 holds a reference (an address) to the object on the heap. If you write Student s2 = s1; you do not get a second student. Both variables point at the same object, so changing it through s2 changes what s1 sees. Beginners get burned by this constantly.

static vs instance

Instance members belong to each object (every student has their own name). A static member belongs to the class itself and is shared (a counter of how many students exist). Static methods cannot touch instance fields because there is no object to ask.

Exam checklist for a class question

Is the class public? Are all fields private? Does each constructor use this? Did you write getters? Did you read the access word of each sub-question (public, private, or no modifier for package-only)? Do you have a main that creates objects and calls methods?

quiz.q: A class is best described as?
quiz.why: The class is the plan, the object is the thing built from it.

quiz.q: What is wrong with: public void Student(String n) { name = n; } as a constructor?
options: It has a void return type, so it is an ordinary method
quiz.why: Constructors have no return type at all.

quiz.q: In the constructor, name = name; (no this) does what?
options: Assigns the parameter to itself and leaves the field unset
quiz.why: Without this, both names mean the parameter.

quiz.q: Student s2 = s1; then s2.setGpa(1.0). What happens to s1's gpa?
quiz.why: Both variables reference the same object.

quiz.q: You write only Student(String n). Can you still call new Student()?
options: No, the free default constructor disappears
quiz.why: Writing any constructor removes the automatic empty one.

options: To protect data behind controlled getters and setters

quiz.q: Which can a static method access directly?
quiz.why: No object exists for a static method, so no instance fields and no this.

quiz.q: Which access modifier means 'only inside the same package'?

lab.task: Write a class BankAccount with a private balance, a constructor taking the opening balance, deposit(amount) that rejects negatives, withdraw(amount) that refuses to go below zero and returns true or false, and getBalance(). Then in main, create two accounts and show they are independent.
